n: Jesus has called twelve disciples with authority to baptize. He tells the crowd they are blessed if they follow these Twelve, are baptized by them with water, and then receive His baptism of fire and the Holy Ghost. Those who have seen Him and believe are blessed.

f.w: baptize you with fire and with the Holy Ghost

n: Even more blessed are those who believe without seeing, through the testimony of these witnesses, and humbly accept baptism. This blessing reaches all later believers, including us.

f.w: more blessed are they who shall believe in your words

n: The Beatitudes begin, much as in Matthew 5. Here Jesus adds “who come unto me”: being humble in spirit is the start, coming to Christ completes it. Such people receive the kingdom of heaven.

f.g: Humble, aware of one’s spiritual need.
Not in Matthew 5:3; the Book of Mormon ties the blessing to coming to Christ.

n: Those who mourn, whether for sin, loss, or suffering, will be comforted.
The meek, gentle and teachable rather than weak, will inherit the earth.
Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness will be filled. Here the Book of Mormon specifies: “filled with the Holy Ghost.”

f.g: Matthew 5:6 says only “filled”; this version names what fills them.

n: The merciful will receive mercy. How we treat others shapes how we are treated.
The pure in heart will see God, a promise fulfilled literally for this very crowd.
Peacemakers will be called God’s children because they act like Him.
Those persecuted for Christ’s sake will have the kingdom of heaven.

f.g: Matthew 5:10 says “for righteousness’ sake”; here the focus is on loyalty to Christ.

n: Blessed are those insulted, persecuted, and falsely accused because of Christ.

f.g: Insult; speak abusively against.

n: They should rejoice, because their heavenly reward will be great, and the prophets before them were treated the same way.
Jesus makes His disciples the salt of the earth. Salt that loses its flavor is useless and thrown out. Disciples must keep their distinct goodness to bless the world.

f.g: Flavor; taste.

n: They are to be the light of this people, like a city on a hill that cannot be hidden.

f.w: A city that is set on a hill

n: No one lights a lamp and covers it with a basket; they set it on a stand to light the whole house.

f.g: A basket or container for measuring grain.
A lampstand.

n: So let your light shine so that others see your good works and praise the Father, not you.
Jesus did not come to destroy the law or the prophets, but to fulfill them.

f.w: not come to destroy but to fulfil

n: Not the smallest detail of the law has been lost, but it has all been fulfilled in Him. This differs from Matthew, where fulfillment is still future; after the Resurrection, Christ speaks of it as complete.

f.w: in me it hath all been fulfilled
f.g: Matthew 5:18 says “till all be fulfilled.”
The smallest Hebrew letter.

n: He has given them the Father’s commandments: believe in Him, repent, and come to Him with a broken heart and contrite spirit. The law is fulfilled, and these commandments now guide them.

f.w: a broken heart and a contrite spirit

n: So come to Him and be saved, but they must keep His present commandments to enter heaven. This replaces Matthew 5:19-20’s comparison with the scribes and Pharisees.

f.w: except ye shall keep my commandments

n: Jesus begins a series of contrasts. The old law said do not kill, and killers face judgment.

f.g: The ancients; earlier generations under the law of Moses.

n: But anger itself brings judgment. Contemptuous insults like “Raca” (empty-head) or “fool” bring greater danger still. Unlike most Bible manuscripts, this version omits “without a cause,” forbidding anger altogether.

f.g: An Aramaic insult meaning roughly “empty-headed” or “worthless.”
The local court or ruling body.
The Joseph Smith Translation of Matthew likewise drops “without a cause.”

n: If you come or want to come to Christ and remember someone has something against you...

f.g: Anything.

n: ...go and make peace first, then come to Him wholeheartedly, and He will receive you. In Matthew it’s bringing a gift to the altar; here, with sacrifices ended, it’s coming to Christ.

f.w: first be reconciled to thy brother

n: Settle disputes with your opponent quickly while you can, before it ends with you in prison.

f.g: Opponent, here in a legal dispute.

n: You won’t get out until you pay the last “senine,” the smallest Nephite coin. Jesus uses a local unit instead of the Roman farthing in Matthew. And in prison you can’t earn even one.

f.g: A Nephite measure of value, the smallest listed.

n: The old law said do not commit adultery.
But looking on someone with lust is already adultery in the heart. Christ’s law reaches thoughts, not just actions.

f.w: hath committed adultery already in his heart

n: Don’t let these things enter your heart at all. This replaces Matthew’s graphic image of plucking out an eye or cutting off a hand.

f.w: suffer none of these things to enter into your heart
f.g: Compare Matthew 5:29-30; the Book of Mormon states the principle directly.

n: It is better to deny yourself these things, taking up your cross, than to be cast into hell. Self-control is a form of discipleship.
The law allowed a man to divorce his wife by giving her a written certificate.
Jesus raises the standard: divorce except for sexual unfaithfulness leads to adultery, and so does marrying a divorced person. Marriage is meant to be lasting.

f.w: saving for the cause of fornication

n: The old law said not to break oaths made to the Lord.

f.g: Swear falsely; break an oath.

n: Jesus says don’t swear oaths at all, not by heaven, which is God’s throne...
...nor by the earth, His footstool...
...nor by your own head, since you can’t even change the color of one hair.
Just let your “yes” mean yes and your “no” mean no. A truthful person needs no oaths.
The law said “an eye for an eye,” a principle that originally limited revenge to fair compensation.
But Jesus says don’t retaliate. If struck on the right cheek, an insulting backhand, turn the other. Answer insult with patience.

f.w: turn to him the other also

n: If someone sues for your coat, give your cloak too, going beyond what is demanded.

f.g: The inner garment, a tunic.
The outer garment, which under the law could not be kept overnight.

n: If forced to carry a load one mile, as Roman soldiers could require, go two. Generosity turns compulsion into service.

f.g: Two.

n: Give to those who ask, and don’t turn away those who want to borrow.

f.w: Give to him that asketh thee

n: It was said, love your neighbor and hate your enemy. (The law commands loving neighbors; hating enemies was a common attitude, not a written command.)
Jesus says: love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you.

f.g: Spitefully; with malice.

n: This is how you become like your Father in heaven, who lets His sun rise on both the evil and the good.

f.w: he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good

n: The things of old under the law are all fulfilled in Him. This verse is unique to the Book of Mormon version.
Old things are done away, and all things have become new, a new covenant and a new way of life in Christ.
Be perfect, even as Christ or the Father is perfect. Unlike Matthew 5:48, the resurrected Jesus now includes Himself. “Perfect” suggests complete and whole, a goal reached through Christ.

f.g: Matthew mentions only the Father; now resurrected, Christ names Himself as perfected.
